# Laya Triage

<!-- Generated by docs/make_readme.py from docs/README.template.md and files under results/ and config/; do not edit by hand. -->

**Label new GitHub issues as `bug`, `feature` or `question`, and only when the model is confident.**
A GitHub Action that runs a fine-tuned [Laya]({{laya_url}}) decision model on the runner's CPU. No server, no API key, no paid service.

## What and why

Maintainers spend time reading each new issue just to decide what kind it is. Keyword bots are brittle. LLM bots are slow, cost money per call, return free text and give no trustworthy confidence. Laya Triage cleans the issue title and body, asks a fine-tuned Laya model one typed question ("what kind of issue is this?") and reads calibrated probabilities for the three labels from a single forward pass. If the top label's probability reaches that label's threshold, the Action applies the label. Otherwise it adds `{{escalate_label}}` and, if you opt in, posts a short comment with the top two guesses. In dry-run mode, the default, it only writes its decisions to the job summary.

Where it stands, in one paragraph: on the NLBSE'24 test split the model reaches cross-repo macro-F1 **{{test_xrepo}}** (the TF-IDF baseline reaches {{b1_xrepo}}, the published SetFit baseline {{setfit_xrepo}}). The confidence gate is the weak part. With the shipped thresholds it auto-labels {{gate_cov_pct}} of test issues, only `bug`, at precision {{gate_prec_pct}}, so it **{{target_status}} the {{target}} precision target**. Read [Results](#results) and [Limitations](#limitations), and watch dry-run output on your own repository, before you switch to `apply`.

## Quick start

### Add the workflow

Save this as `.github/workflows/laya-triage.yml`. It triages new issues, supports a manual backfill, and warms the caches twice a week:

```yaml
{{consumer_workflow}}
```

The job needs `issues: write` and `contents: read`, nothing else. `{{tag}}` is a tag, and tags can move: for anything beyond a trial, replace it with the full commit SHA of the release and keep the tag as a comment (`uses: Prasanna-KS-85/laya-triage@<full commit SHA> # {{tag}}`; see §7.6 of `PROJECT_SPEC.md`). The Action runs on Linux X64 only. It was tested on `ubuntu-24.04`; `ubuntu-latest` moves to a newer image on {{ubuntu_switch_date}}, so pin `ubuntu-24.04` if you want the tested one.

### Create the labels

The Action skips a label that does not exist, unless you set `behaviour.create_missing_labels`:

```bash
{{label_cmds}}
```

### Warm the caches once

In the Actions tab, run the workflow manually with `warm-cache` ticked. It validates the config, loads the model and saves the model and dependency caches, but reads no issues and makes no GitHub API call. Issues-triggered runs can restore these caches but cannot save them, which is why the schedule in the example exists.

### Stay in dry-run and read the job summaries

The default mode is `{{mode}}`. Open a few issues, or run the workflow manually with a `backfill-count` to classify the most recent open issues, then read the decision table in each run's job summary: label, probabilities, and whether the Action would apply or escalate. Compare it with what you would have done.

### Switch to apply

Only when you are happy with what dry-run showed, add `.github/laya-triage.yml`:

```yaml
behaviour:
  mode: apply
```

With the shipped thresholds ({{thresholds_text}}), only `bug` is ever applied automatically. `feature` and `question` are always escalated, because no threshold on validation data reached the precision target for them (a threshold of {{never}} means never).

## How it works

1. **Preprocess.** One shared function strips HTML comments, collapses long code blocks and logs, replaces images and bare URLs with placeholders, normalises whitespace and caps the body. The state is `{"title": ..., "body": ...}`. Training, evaluation and the Action all call the same function.
2. **Laya question.** The state goes to the fine-tuned model together with one typed `choice` question whose options are {{labels_list}}. The wording and the option order are frozen: the options are part of the model's input, so changing them changes its behaviour.
3. **Calibrated probabilities.** One forward pass on CPU (fp32) gives a probability per label. Gating uses `answer_confidence`, the probability of the chosen label, never the entropy-based `confidence`.
4. **Per-label thresholds.** Each label has its own threshold, fitted on validation data as the smallest value whose bootstrap lower bound of precision is at least {{target}}; {{never}} means the label is never auto-applied.
5. **Apply or escalate.** At or above the threshold the label is applied; otherwise the escalation label is added. In dry-run, nothing changes and the decision goes to the job summary.

The model is Laya (a ModernBERT-large encoder with a small decision head), fine-tuned with Laya's RLCD recipe (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions) on {{n_train}} NLBSE'24 training rows: the official training set minus {{n_dropped}} rows whose content also appears in test, minus {{n_val}} validation issues. The choice temperature was then refit on those validation issues ({{T_notebook}} to {{T_val}}); the weights are unchanged. The model card is at [{{model_repo}}]({{hf_url}}), pinned in the default config to revision `{{revision}}`.

## Results

Test split of the NLBSE'24 issue report classification benchmark: {{n_test}} issues, {{per_cell}} per class in each of {{n_repos}} repositories, each judged by a protocol declared in advance. That evaluation was run once, after the thresholds were frozen. Exploratory analyses run later reused the test predictions and are labelled post-hoc (`results/phase3.md`). The headline metric is **cross-repo macro-F1**, the mean of the per-repository macro-F1 scores, as in the competition. Every number below is generated from the files under `results/` (mainly `results/phase3/test_R1b/metrics_test.json`).

| System | Cross-repo macro-F1 | Pooled macro-F1 | Accuracy | F1 bug | F1 feature | F1 question | ECE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
{{results_table}}

[c] Derived, not published: NLBSE'24 publishes per-repository, per-class precision, recall and F1, and the pooled values were recovered exactly from them because every test repository has {{per_cell}} issues per class. B3 publishes no probabilities, so it has no ECE.

**This is not a like-for-like comparison with B3.** B3 trains one classifier per repository, each on only that repository's {{b3_rows_per_clf}} official-train rows (together the {{n_repos}} classifiers use all {{n_official}} rows, including the {{n_dropped}} whose content also appears in test). The SetFit baseline's input is the raw title and body; the RoBERTa and fastText training setups were not inspected. B3 is copied from the competition repository, not re-run. M1 and B1 are one model across all {{n_repos}} repositories, trained on {{n_train}} rows, and M1's temperature and thresholds (and B1's hyperparameters) were fitted on a {{n_val}}-issue validation split. B2 is the base checkpoint without fine-tuning. On the headline metric M1 is {{setfit_cmp}} SetFit and {{roberta_cmp}} RoBERTa.

**Paired comparisons** (same test issues): difference in cross-repo macro-F1 with a {{ci_level}}% confidence interval from a paired bootstrap ({{n_boot}} resamples of issues, seed {{seed}}), and the exact McNemar p-value. M1 {{beats}}, and {{ci_text}}.

| Comparison | Δ cross-repo macro-F1 | {{ci_level}}% CI | McNemar p |
|---|---:|---|---:|
{{paired_table}}

**Calibration** (expected calibration error, {{ece_bins}} bins). T is the temperature that divides the logits; T = 1 is the uncalibrated model. The success criterion was a test ECE of at most {{ece_limit}}; it is {{ece_status}}.

| Probabilities | ECE | Brier |
|---|---:|---:|
{{calib_table}}

**Gating at the shipped thresholds.** Thresholds were fitted on validation before the test run, and test was not used to change them.

| Label | Threshold | Val lower bound | Applied on test | Test coverage | Test precision |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
{{gating_table}}
| **all** | | | {{gate_applied}} of {{gate_n}} | **{{gate_cov}}** | **{{gate_prec}}** |

**The {{target}} precision target was {{target_status}} on test.** On validation the `bug` threshold had precision {{bug_val_prec}} (bootstrap lower bound {{bug_val_lb}}, {{bug_val_n}} issues, in-sample); on test the same threshold gave {{bug_test_prec}}, {{bug_prec_loss}} points lower. `feature` and `question` never reached the lower bound on validation, so they are always escalated: on test the target was met for {{met_k}} of {{n_labels}} labels (on validation {{val_bound_labels}} a {{target}} bootstrap lower bound). For comparison, the point-estimate thresholds from validation would auto-label {{point_cov}} of test issues at precision {{point_prec}}, and the TF-IDF baseline, gated with its own validation-fitted thresholds, auto-labelled {{b1_gate_cov}} of test issues at precision {{b1_gate_prec}}.

![Coverage against precision of M1 on the test split]({{figure_path}})

The curve shows precision against coverage when one global threshold is varied. It describes the test split only, so it must not be used to pick a threshold. The shipped operating point is the one at coverage {{gate_cov}}.

## Runtime on GitHub-hosted runners

Measured on an `ubuntu-24.04` runner in a private sandbox repository ({{runner_cpus}} logical CPUs, {{runner_cpu_model}}, {{runner_ram_mib}} MiB of RAM). Details and run ids are in `results/phase4.md`.

| Scenario | Wall time | Target | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Issue run, both caches cold (first run) | {{cold}} | ≤ {{nfr3}} (NFR-3) | {{nfr3_status}} |
| Issue run, both caches restored | {{warm}} | ≤ {{nfr2}} (NFR-2) | {{nfr2_status}} |
| `warm-cache` run from cold caches (saves both caches) | {{warm_cache}} | | |
| Manual run that saved both caches and ran the latency probe | {{cold_dispatch}} | | |

**Per-issue inference (NFR-1): {{nfr1_status}}.** The probe classified the sandbox fixtures {{probe_n}} times with the model already loaded, on {{probe_threads}} torch thread: p50 {{probe_p50}}, p95 {{probe_p95}}, against a target of p95 ≤ {{nfr1}} on a hosted runner. Treat the figure with care:

- The fixtures are not a sample of real issues. They include a long log and several near-empty issues, so the tail is set by a few long inputs.
- It is one run on one runner instance, and hosted-runner hardware and neighbours vary.
- Torch ran single-threaded, so it says nothing about a machine with more cores. For reference only, on {{local_hw}} (model preloaded, {{local_threads}} threads) the full test run measured p50 {{local_p50}} and p95 {{local_p95}}; that is a different machine and not comparable.
- A length-matched probe, built from synthetic texts that follow the validation length distribution, would give a better estimate; it is on the roadmap.

NFR-1 is {{nfr1_status}} on this runner. The planned remedy is v1.2: export the model to ONNX INT8, compare accuracy, ECE and latency with the torch backend, and switch `model.backend` only if it is better.

## Limitations

- **English only, and no language guard.** The model was trained and evaluated on English issues. A German fixture in the sandbox (S17) was labelled `bug` with `answer_confidence` {{s17_conf}}, above the `bug` threshold of {{s17_tau}}, so it would be labelled `bug` in apply mode.
- **Issue text can steer the label.** A fixture that asks to be labelled a feature (S18) was predicted `feature` with {{s18_conf}}. The damage is bounded: the output is one of three labels, no issue text is executed or repeated in comments, and with the default thresholds `feature` is never auto-applied (its threshold is {{s18_tau}}), so that issue was escalated. With the default thresholds the label an author can steer towards is {{auto_label}}, the only auto-applied label (S17 shows a non-English issue reaching it), and a wrong {{auto_label}} label is a mistake a maintainer can remove. A repository that lowers the `feature` threshold removes the protection for `feature`.
- **Balanced training data, random split, {{n_repos}} repositories.** Test has exactly {{per_cell}} issues per class per repository and the training rows are near-balanced ({{train_counts}}). Real repositories have very different class mixes, the split is random rather than temporal, and the data come from {{n_repos}} large projects only. Precision at a given threshold will differ elsewhere.
- **Label noise**, especially for `question`, the weakest class (test F1 {{question_f1}}). Labels come from the upstream repositories' own labels. See the manual review of training rows in [data/DATA_CARD.md](data/DATA_CARD.md).
- **Validation overstated test performance.** Cross-repo macro-F1 was {{val_xrepo}} on the {{n_val}}-issue validation split and {{test_xrepo}} on test. A check for near-duplicates between training and evaluation issues (TF-IDF cosine similarity) rules out one explanation: the share of issues above {{near_cut}} similarity to a training issue is {{near_val_share}} on validation and {{near_test_share}} on test, and M1's accuracy fell from validation to test in every similarity tertile (by {{tertile_drops}} points). M1 was fine-tuned once (there was no choice among runs on validation), so the drop is not selection among models. The cause is not identified; sampling noise on {{n_val}} issues is one candidate.
- **Thresholds fitted on {{n_val}} validation issues do not transfer exactly.** The `bug` threshold lost {{bug_prec_loss}} points of precision from validation to test, and that is why the precision target was {{target_status}}.
- **Truncation.** {{share_truncated}} of test issues are longer than {{max_len}} tokens after cleaning; the text beyond that is not seen.
- **Issues-triggered runs cannot write caches** (the cache write is refused for that token). Caches are saved by `schedule` and `workflow_dispatch` runs, which is what the `warm-cache` input and the example schedule are for. GitHub may evict a cache that is unused for a week, and the next run is then cold.
- **Dataset license unspecified.** The upstream NLBSE'24 repository has an empty `LICENSE` file, so no license is granted for the data. This repository never contains the raw data; `training/fetch_data.py` downloads it from the upstream commit and verifies its SHA-256. See `data/DATA_CARD.md`.

## Reproduce

Everything below runs from the repository root. The raw data and the model weights are not in the repository.

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[dev,eval]"
.venv/bin/python training/fetch_data.py       # NLBSE'24 CSVs at the pinned upstream commit, SHA-256 checked
.venv/bin/python training/build_dataset.py    # splits, training and evaluation rows, manifests; asserts the data checks
```

**Train** with `training/finetune_kaggle.ipynb` on Kaggle ({{kaggle_gpus}}× T4, internet on, {{epochs}} epochs). The notebook is generated by `training/build_notebook.py`, embeds `training/make_items.py`, and checks the hash of the training items against `results/phase3/items_sha256.json` before it trains. It pushes to a Hugging Face repository you must create first; point the run config at your own. The run ledger is `results/experiments.md`.

**Evaluate** on CPU in fp32 (evaluation here used Python {{eval_python}}):

```bash
.venv/bin/python eval/baselines.py run --split val        # B0, B1, B2; `report` summarises
.venv/bin/python eval/run_eval.py --model-repo <repo> --revision <sha> --split val --expect-max-len {{max_len}} --expect-head-max-len {{head_max_len}} --tag M1_<run>
.venv/bin/python results/phase3/refit_temperature.py      # refit the choice temperature on validation
.venv/bin/python results/phase3/val_report.py --run <run> --write-config   # thresholds (§10.4) -> config/triage.default.yml
```

**The test-once rule.** Test is run once per frozen model and config. `eval/run_eval.py` refuses `--split test` unless `config/triage.default.yml` is committed and unmodified, its revision and `max_len` match the command line, the tag has no test predictions yet, and the test file has its pinned SHA-256. The pre-declared command, exactly as it was run (see `results/phase3.md`, "Test protocol"):

```bash
{{test_command}}
```

Then `results/phase3/test_report.py` computes the metrics, the paired comparisons and the figures from the saved predictions. To rebuild this README and the model card from those files: `.venv/bin/python docs/make_readme.py` and `.venv/bin/python results/phase3/make_model_card.py`. Unit tests, which download no weights: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -m "not slow"`.

## How this was built

- **Spec-driven.** `PROJECT_SPEC.md` is the single source of truth, from requirements and architecture to the data splits, thresholds procedure and risks. Where code and spec disagree the spec wins until it is deliberately changed, and every change is in its changelog. Coding agents (Claude Code) worked from `CLAUDE.md`, which points to the spec and its rules.
- **Pre-registered test protocol.** Before any test prediction of the model existed, the metrics to report, the comparisons and the pass/fail judgement of each success criterion were written down in `results/phase3.md` ("Test protocol (pre-declared)"). The thresholds were committed first, test was run once, and misses are reported as misses: the precision target and NFR-1 are both in this README. Anything run after seeing test numbers is labelled post-hoc and changes no criterion.
- **Phases with gates and tags.** The work went in phases (feasibility, dataset, baselines, fine-tuning, the Action, release), each ending with a verification gate and a git tag (`phase0-complete` and so on, then `v1.0.0-rc1`). All numbers in this README and in the model card are generated from files under `results/` (spec rule 11), not typed.

## Roadmap

- **v1.1:** a language guard that escalates non-English issues instead of classifying them; the `needs_info` flag from the spec's release map; a length-matched latency probe; a hash-pinned dependency lock; an optional formatting pass that leaves the frozen files alone.
- **v1.2:** ONNX INT8 export and `model.backend: onnx`, aimed at the NFR-1 target.
- **v2.0 (stretch, not committed):** priority scoring, duplicate suggestions and a `documentation` class.
